description.value: The study examined whether intravenous ghrelin modulates neural responses to visual food cues in healthy nonobese men during fMRI, and whether these effects relate to hunger and recognition of food images.

spans.text: Here, we show that ghrelin administered intravenously to healthy volunteers during functional magnetic resonance imaging increased the neural response to food pictures in regions of the brain, including the amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex, anterior insula, and striatum, implicated in encoding the incentive value of food cues.

design.value: Twenty healthy medication-free normal weight male subjects were studied 3 hr after a standardized meal. Twelve subjects underwent control and ghrelin blocks, while eight underwent two control blocks without ghrelin; all subjects viewed food and scenery images during fMRI.

spans.text: Twenty nonobese subjects were tested 3 hr after ingestion of a standardized meal. Twelve subjects viewed pictures before and after ghrelin administration (control/ghrelin group), and eight subjects viewed the same pictures in two identical blocks without receiving ghrelin (control/control group).
At the start and end of the block, subjects answered questions regarding their mood and appetite (e.g., how hungry are you right now?) on a 10 point visual analog scale.
